abstract: When people think aloud, their reports vary in duration and in how closely successive thoughts are related in meaning. We asked whether these two dimensions relate to distinct patterns of brain dynamics. Using 10-minute think-aloud fMRI scans from 75 adults, we quantified timing as variability in sentence-event duration and semantic continuity as similarity between adjacent grouped thoughts. In models including both measures, greater duration variability was associated with lower relative brain entropy (BEN), estimated from BOLD time series, in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (voxel wise FDR q < 0.05). This association persisted after adjustment for speech coverage, pause duration, articulation rate and event count. Semantic continuity was associated with differences in BOLD amplitude and synchrony across bilateral sensorimotor regions. These voxel wise associations fell below the FDR threshold after adjustment for speech coverage or pause duration. In a secondary atlas-based analysis, semantic continuity remained positively associated with local synchrony in Default C after adjustment for speech timing ({beta} = 0.517, P = 0.003). These findings link the timing of spoken reports to dorsolateral prefrontal brain activity irregularity and show how the sensorimotor correlates of semantic continuity covary with speech timing.
